lead.kicker: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah on technological progress
lead.head: Moore makes more, for less

pic.caption: Ajay Shah (left) and Amit Varma early in Episode 87

body: The episode began with an exam. Amit Varma asked Ajay Shah for the sum of the squares of the first four primes. Shah added aloud, landed on 87, and the episode had its num­ber. {087-J01}

Then Shah had to pitch his topic like a job ap­pli­cant. His sub­ject was Moore’s Laws, plu­ral, and what fol­lowed was a con­ver­sa­tion on why the mod­ern world keeps get­ting bet­ter and cheaper, and what that says about peo­ple.
## A so­cial fact

Moore’s Law, in Shah’s bumper-sticker ver­sion, says the num­ber of tran­sis­tors on a chip dou­bles every 18 months or so. Gordon Moore saw the pat­tern in a 1965 paper that rested on seven data points.
The Intel 4004, the first CPU on a sin­gle chip, did the whole job with about 2,300 tran­sis­tors. Our phones now squan­der bil­lions.

Nothing in na­ture guar­an­tees the dou­bling, Shah stressed. “This is not a physics law,” he said. “It’s not a phys­i­cal fact about the uni­verse. It’s a so­cial fact. It’s an eco­nomic fact.” {087-C02}

Draw it with time on one axis and a log scale on the other, and the dou­bling be­comes a straight line. Shah’s phrase for it, which re­curred through the episode, was “straight lines on a semi-log graph”.
## The plu­ral
Billions of tran­sis­tors would be a cu­rios­ity, Shah said, if each chip cost a mil­lion dol­lars. The more im­por­tant ver­sion of the law, per­haps five times more, puts price on the y-axis.

The same straight lines turn up in solar pan­els, band­width, lithium-ion bat­ter­ies, DNA se­quenc­ing and the cost of send­ing a kilo into orbit. “As an econ­o­mist, I just want to say that’s the whole en­chi­lada,” he said. “You’ve got to get the prices down.” {087-C03}

Then came two rival laws. Wright’s Law, from 1936, puts life­time out­put on the x-axis: roughly a 20 per cent pro­duc­tiv­ity gain for every dou­bling. Goddard’s Law cred­its an­nual scale. A study of 62 in­dus­tries, Shah said, found Wright’s the best pre­dic­tor.
“Not time. Volume,” he said. “You put in vol­ume and you will get im­prove­ments.”
Varma drew a les­son for cre­ators: do, do, do. Shah added the caveat that the gains are a fron­tier, earned only by firms that work at them.
## A shared re­li­gion

The law also solves a puz­zle, Shah ar­gued. A chip needs ASML’s ma­chines in Holland, American de­sign soft­ware, thou­sands of en­gi­neers in Bangalore and hun­dreds of other firms. No gov­ern­ment co­or­di­nates them.

Instead the in­dus­try “signed up for the re­li­gion” of the 18-month dou­bling, so each firm dared to in­vest ahead of the rest. “It be­came a co­or­di­na­tion mech­a­nism by hun­dreds of firms,” he said. {087-C12}
Varma’s gloss was that the ar­tic­u­la­tion of the law mat­ters as much as the law: a shared dream makes ac­tion look co­or­di­nated when it is not.
For Varma the deeper story was human: peo­ple, he said, are brains, not stom­achs.

Near the end, Shah made a con­fes­sion. He had un­der­rated dig­i­tal cam­eras and lithium-ion bat­ter­ies, even as an en­thu­si­ast. “Humans are not good at ex­po­nen­tial think­ing,” he said. {087-C14}
Varma’s ad­vice to young en­trepreneurs fol­lowed from it: “Make for the fu­ture. Don’t make for today.”

second.label: The Ehrlich–Simon bet
second.head: Simon says: prices fall
second.deck: Amit Varma on a 1980 wager between gloom and ingenuity
body: Paul Ehrlich made Malthusian pre­dic­tions, Amit Varma said. In the early sev­en­ties he said Britain would be ex­tinct by 2000, and that half of India would starve by the end of the decade. {#ehrlich}

Julian Simon, whom Varma called a great econ­o­mist, found such claims ridicu­lous. In 1980 the two bet on the prices of five ma­te­ri­als, cho­sen by Ehrlich, over ten years. If pop­u­la­tion rose and re­sources did not, Malthusian logic said prices would rise. {087-S08}
All five fell, and Simon won. “We kept in­no­vat­ing, we kept doing funky things,” Varma said. For him the bet is ev­i­dence that peo­ple are brains, not stom­achs. {087-C16}

quote.text: Julian Simon was like, No, hold on, man. We are in­no­va­tive, we are cre­ative, that is a core of progress.

third.head: Make ten pots, not one

pic.caption: Amit Varma on ten pots a day

body: Amit Varma cited an ex­per­i­ment whose de­tails, he ad­mit­ted, he had for­got­ten. One group had a month to make a sin­gle per­fect pot. {#pots} The other had to make ten pots a day, and their best would be judged.
The perfectionists’ pot came out medi­ocre. The vol­ume group quickly passed that stan­dard and went on to make re­ally good pots.

For Varma, this is Wright’s Law for the cre­ator econ­omy. Many cre­ators get stuck chas­ing the per­fect blog, the per­fect YouTube show, the per­fect episode. “The key to ex­cel­lence is not to spend for­ever over try­ing to make some­thing per­fect, but doing, doing, doing, doing, doing,” he said. {087-C08}
Do that, and “your base­line level gets so high that ex­cel­lence au­to­mat­i­cally emerges”. {087-S04}

p2.deck: Moore’s Law, its plural, two rival laws and the faith that keeps an industry in step

quote.text: It’s an eco­nomic law that we are able to pile on the in­no­va­tions and the cap­i­tal in­ten­sity

photo.caption: Intel co-founder Gordon Moore in his Santa Clara office in 2003

box.title: The man behind the law
box.text: Gordon Moore set out the law in a 1965 paper using just seven data points. “All you need is seven good data points to get a world chang­ing ob­ser­va­tion,” Ajay Shah said. The law, he stressed, is eco­nom­ics, not physics. {087-C02}

sections.label: The first law
sections.head: Seven dots and a straight line
sections.caption: the law that isn’t physics
body: The tran­sis­tor, Ajay Shah said, is a thing with three prongs, first made in 1947 and as­sem­bled by hand at Bell Labs. Then came the pres­sure to do more, and the most im­por­tant cus­tomers were in space re­search.

NASA was des­per­ate to put small, com­pact equip­ment on satel­lites. {#nasa} Its fund­ing, Shah said, lit­er­ally cre­ated the in­dus­try: in­te­grated cir­cuits, then very large scale in­te­gra­tion, then the Intel 4004.
That chip had some­thing like 2,300 tran­sis­tors, a fig­ure Shah of­fered to “all ye cal­low gen­tle read­ers” who squan­der bil­lions on their phones. {087-J05}
## Fetch, add, branch
At heart, he ex­plained, a CPU is a Turing ma­chine. It needs to fetch a mem­ory cell into a reg­is­ter, to add, and to branch on an if. “Everything else is top­pings.” {087-C01}

Gordon Moore saw the pat­tern in seven com­po­nents and hy­poth­e­sised about what was going on. The dou­bling, roughly every 18 months, has run for decades since. Plotted on a semi-log graph, it gives a ten­fold rise every few years.

Amit Varma reached for the old para­ble of the king and the chess­board: one grain of rice on the first square, dou­bled on each square after. Shah worked out the total in kilo­grams against the mass of the earth and de­clared it “well be­yond the re­sources of any king”.
~ Varma was un­moved. “Doesn’t mat­ter,” he said. “It’s a lot of grain.” {087-J04}

quote.text: It’s an eco­nomic law that we are able to pile on the in­no­va­tions and the cap­i­tal in­ten­sity

sections.label: What it did
sections.head: When engineering became code
sections.caption: cheap chips everywhere
body: Computation be­came ubiq­ui­tous and cheap, Ajay Shah said. A mind-blowing CPU can cost a dol­lar or ten cents, cheap enough to waste. You can put one in a toaster.

That turned old tri­umphs of me­chan­i­cal en­gi­neer­ing into triv­ial soft­ware. Cruise con­trol, which holds Shah’s car at the 100 kph limit on the Mumbai Trans Harbour Link, once needed very clever peo­ple. Now it is a few lines: push the speed up below 99, down above 101. {087-C04}
## Leaps and grind­ing

Not all progress is like this. Lighting went from can­dles to gas lamps, tung­sten, flu­o­res­cent tubes and LEDs, from about 9 per cent ef­fi­ciency to 90. But it came in jumps be­tween stag­na­tions, and that jour­ney, Shah said, is now over. {087-C05}
Amit Varma saw two kinds of learn­ing in this: steady ac­cu­mu­la­tion, or a leap, then re­fine­ment, then an­other leap.

More tran­sis­tors did not even make CPUs faster. Built on the sin­gle-threaded PDP-11 model, they mostly sat wait­ing for mem­ory. Tricks such as com­put­ing both sides of an if squeezed out about ten­fold, then maxed out. The GPU, a thou­sand small pro­ces­sors on one chip, was the way through.

~ Varma, who calls him­self the best driver in Bombay thanks partly to au­to­matic trans­mis­sion, asked whether man­ual ver­sus au­to­matic was a ques­tion “akin to the Oxford comma and the semi­colon”. {087-J06}

quote.text: What we are de­scrib­ing as Moore’s Law is just this mad­ness of grind­ing away year after year, the damn thing gets bet­ter.

sections.label: Moore’s Laws
sections.head: Cheaper by the doubling
sections.caption: price on the y-axis
body: Technology is a great equaliser, Amit Varma ar­gued, against those on the left who say it widens in­equal­ity. It starts with gov­ern­ments or the rich and reaches ev­ery­one, and fall­ing prices are what carry it there. {087-C15}

Ajay Shah took up the point, and ex­plained the plu­ral in the episode’s title. Put price, or per­for­mance per price, on the y-axis and the straight lines ap­pear again. Solar pan­els began as ex­otic kit on satel­lites. {#solar} Their rival there, the plu­to­nium bat­tery, never got the same price gains.
## A uni­ver­sity on one line

When Shah was a PhD stu­dent in America, the whole University of Southern California ran on a T1 line of about 1.5 megabits a sec­ond, “the height of cool”. Today a home con­nec­tion gives some­thing like 300, for less. {087-S02}
Launch costs fell in the six­ties and sev­en­ties, then stag­nated for a long time. Now pri­vate firms are in­no­vat­ing again, and peo­ple pre­dict $10 a kilo to near-earth orbit. {#tenkg}

Varma re­mem­bered dial-up: the sound of the modem, and “half a pic­ture of Samantha Fox” be­fore the line dropped. Shah went one bet­ter: he could hear the modem ne­go­ti­ate and tell which pro­to­col it got through. {087-J07}
~ Today, Varma said, broad­band is ef­fec­tively free and ef­fec­tively ev­ery­where.

quote.text: The cell phone that I use is not very dif­fer­ent from the cell phone Elon Musk uses.

sections.label: Two more laws
sections.head: Volume, not the calendar
sections.caption: Wright’s Law and the learning curve
body: Ajay Shah of­fered two ri­vals to Moore’s Law. Wright’s Law, from 1936, by a man who was not one of the Wright broth­ers, says pro­duc­tiv­ity rises with life­time vol­ume, about 20 per cent for every dou­bling. Goddard’s Law cred­its scale in a sin­gle year. {087-C07}

Nagy and col­leagues tested them across 62 in­dus­tries and found Wright’s the best. So, Shah said, judge a per­son by life­time out­put: a cob­bler who has re­paired 53,000 shoes is “stand­ing on some­thing great”. {#cobbler}
Amit Varma ap­plied it to the show: by episode 174 they would be 20 per cent bet­ter. Shah agreed, but noted the learn­ing rate had al­ready slowed. {087-J08}
## Why firms stall

The gains are not pre­or­dained, Shah warned. Bad firms run con­sul­tant-chosen ma­chines like help­less peas­ants and wait for the next up­grade. They churn their teams, so tacit knowl­edge walks out. And they are cut to the bone, with no slack for think­ing or mis­takes. {087-C11}
He cited a line from *Even Cowgirls Get the Blues*: the only peo­ple on rou­tine flights are those who think they are on rou­tine flights. {087-R09}
~ Varma added Anders Ericsson’s idea of de­lib­er­ate prac­tice: vol­ume works only when you think about what you are doing.

quote.text: But when you lack the fat, think­ing, for strat­egy, for in­no­va­tion, for mak­ing mis­takes. Then ac­tu­ally you don’t get on these jour­neys to qual­ity.

sections.label: I, CPU
sections.head: No planner, no problem
sections.caption: an industry that coordinates itself
body: Amit Varma raised Leonard Read’s essay *I, Pencil*, on how a hum­ble pen­cil needs mil­lions of peo­ple to co­or­di­nate through prices. Ajay Shah upped the stakes: “I, Pencil does not hold a can­dle to I, CPU.” {#pencil}
A chip draws on ASML’s ma­chines in Holland, three American firms’ de­sign soft­ware, tens of thou­sands of en­gi­neers in Bangalore, and ARM, Apple, Intel and hun­dreds more. {#bangalore}

Classic Mahalanobis-style think­ing, Shah said, holds that only a gov­ern­ment could co­erce all of them into step. Yet no gov­ern­ment plays that role. The shared, near-religious be­lief in the 18-month dou­bling does. {087-C12}
## Ten years ahead

ASML saw a decade early that con­ven­tional lithog­ra­phy would max out and that chip­mak­ing would need ex­treme ul­tra­vi­o­let light. Nobody knew how; the physics was se­vere; rival firms failed. ASML kept in­vest­ing for years and got through. {087-S07}
The same faith now funds AI, Shah said, at out­ra­geous cost. A Gemini API call costs about fifty paise, too much for most Indian apps. {#gemini} His chal­lenge: dream of the day it costs 0.05 paise.
~ That, Shah said, is the glory of Moore’s Law: users are told to close their eyes and dream.

quote.text: So Moore’s Law has this very in­ter­est­ing idea that it’s a bit of a self-fulfilling prophecy.

sections.label: The bigger picture
sections.head: From whale oil to the cloud
sections.caption: human ingenuity
body: For Amit Varma, the episode was fi­nally “a hu­man­ity story”. Each time an en­ergy source looked ex­hausted, he said, scarcity raised prices and set off in­no­va­tion: wood gave way to coal, whale oil to fos­sil fuels, and nu­clear and re­new­ables now prom­ise a way be­yond. {087-C16}

Around 2000, big com­pa­nies sank more than $100 bil­lion into fibre-optic cable across America. After the dot-com bust, 90 per cent of it lay un­used, and peo­ple called it a waste. On it came broad­band, mo­bile tele­phony and cloud com­put­ing; today 80 to 90 per cent is in use. {087-S09}
## Missing the curve

Ajay Shah con­fessed his own fail­ures of fore­sight. A hard­core ana­log pho­tog­ra­pher, shoot­ing Kodachrome and Ektachrome on Nikons, he thought early dig­i­tal gear hope­lessly shabby. He was wrong about lithium-ion bat­ter­ies too, de­spite many evenings dream­ing about them with Ayush Patnaik. {087-S10}
His test for any firm: plot pro­duc­tiv­ity against life­time vol­ume on a log scale. No straight line means some­thing is wrong with the or­gan­i­sa­tion and its cul­ture. {087-C10}
~ Varma pointed to Netflix, which bet on stream­ing in 2007 be­fore band­width and dis­plays were ready. Today, he warned, “will be an ar­ti­fact by the time twenty-four hours are over”. {087-C13}

quote.text: And I failed to see that you just have to give it ten, twenty years, and these gaps will be over­come.
Humans are in­cred­i­ble at max­i­miz­ing within their con­straints. As you lift those con­straints, as those bound­aries ex­pand, as ca­pac­ity ex­pands, hu­mans will in­no­vate and fill that space.

p3.title: Tales from the curve
p3.deck: A bankrupting hit, a generous hotel, a phone in Africa, a masterpiece by accident

stories.kicker: Amit Varma’s quiz game of 2000, and its traffic bill
stories.head: Second in India, first in debt
body: In the mid­dle of 2000, the Nasdaq had crashed, the in­vestors in Amit Varma’s first startup had backed out, and *Kaun Banega Crorepati* was just be­com­ing a hit. Varma, a hard­core quizzer, wanted to make some­thing im­mer­sive on­line.

He built Crow Master, a gam­i­fied quiz with a quiz­mas­ter called Babu Moshai, “quite cheesy”, he ad­mit­ted. He paid quizzing friends for a bank of thou­sands of ques­tions. It asked a ques­tion, replied to your an­swer, per­haps of­fered clues, then moved on. It lived on a site called Mindfever.com, along­side other in­ter­ac­tive games.
There was even a way to make money: play­ers could be billed through the tele­phone com­pany, on their phone bills.
Every an­swer pinged the server, so the server had to be close to the play­ers. Varma hosted on VSNL rather than abroad. VSNL charged by traf­fic: the more vis­i­tors, the more you paid.
The game went “madly viral”. For one month it was the num­ber two site in India, some­where be­tween Rediff and Cricinfo. {#numbertwo}
Star’s dig­i­tal arm in Bangalore of­fered to buy it, for a sum Varma half-remembers as fifty lakh or a crore. Then the arm shut down, a ca­su­alty of the Nasdaq crash.

“But that one month bankrupted us and took us hugely into debt be­cause we were pay­ing ac­cord­ing to the traf­fic,” Varma said. {087-S03} The site shut after about three months, and he was left owing a lot of money.
~ None of it ex­ists now, he said, “not even writ­ten about”.
stories.why: Where you sit on the cost curve de­cides whether suc­cess makes you or breaks you. In 2000, every vis­i­tor cost Varma money; today, he said, no one pays for traf­fic that way.
stories.postscript: The first of Varma’s two star­tups, and why it failed, came up in the pre­vi­ous episode.

pic.caption: Amit Varma on the quiz that sank him

stories.kicker: Amit Varma on a hotel that trusted its staff
stories.head: A ring, a laptop, a tank engine
body: Amit Varma had it from a Twitter thread by Ben Wolff. In 1983 Horst Schulze, lead­ing the Ritz-Carlton, let every em­ployee spend up to $2,000 of the hotel’s money on a guest with­out ask­ing any­one. A reg­u­lar guest, he reck­oned, was worth $200,000 over a life­time. {#ritz}

One em­ployee flew from Atlanta to Hawaii to re­turn a guest’s lap­top. A child’s Thomas the Tank Engine, which Varma would not call a toy, came home with pho­to­graphs of Thomas en­joy­ing spa treat­ment.
A cou­ple in Cancun lost their wed­ding ring on the beach the day be­fore the wed­ding. An em­ployee bought four metal de­tec­tors, and staff searched all night until they found it. {#metal}
~ A server over­heard din­ers plan­ning a con­fer­ence at an­other hotel, and comped their $600 din­ner. They moved the con­fer­ence to the Ritz, where it was held every year after. {#comp}

quote.text: $2,000 was a very small amount of money to make peo­ple feel that this was their place.

stories.postscript: Varma’s own case: in 2008, fly­ing back after his mother died, his fam­ily got a free up­grade to busi­ness class at the counter. {087-S06}

pic.caption: Amit Varma on the Ritz-Carlton’s $2,000 rule

stories.kicker: Ajay Shah retells a story from the economist Larry Summers
stories.head: This call is for you
body: Larry Summers, Ajay Shah said, tells a story of the most dra­matic tech­ni­cal change of his life. Shah placed it around the 1992 United States elec­tions, when Summers was an ad­viser to Michael Dukakis and there was a Democratic con­ven­tion, he thought, in Chicago.
A car was sent to pick Summers up, and it had a phone in it. He had never seen a phone in a car. So he picked it up and called his wife: he was call­ing her from a car.
“A scant one and a half years later,” Shah said, Summers was cross­ing a river in Africa when some­body handed him a GSM phone and said: “This call is for you.” {087-S01}
~ That, said Shah, is how the stuff got democra­tised and went all over the world.
stories.why: When a tech­nol­ogy rides a fall­ing price curve, its spread is mea­sured in months, not gen­er­a­tions. That, for Ajay Shah, is why the price ver­sion of Moore’s Law mat­ters: the ex­otic toy be­comes ev­ery­day kit. {087-C03}

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on the phone in the car

stories.kicker: Amit Varma’s recommendation, and the story behind it
stories.head: Sacked band, saved album
body: Van Morrison took a cou­ple of his own mu­si­cians to the stu­dio to record *Astral Weeks*. The pro­ducer, who had his own ideas, quickly sacked them and brought in his own crew, in­clud­ing the bassist Richard Davis.

Morrison sang and played gui­tar while jazz mu­si­cians im­pro­vised around him. “It was a bunch of jazz guys im­pro­vis­ing,” Amit Varma said. “And the re­sult is an ab­so­lute mas­ter­piece.” {087-S11}
Morrison was not happy at first, be­cause it did not match the pic­ture in his head. Over time he came to see it as a mas­ter­piece.

~ Some thirty years later, if Varma re­mem­bered cor­rectly, Morrison toured with Davis and wanted the parts played ex­actly as on the album. Davis, in Varma’s telling, re­fused colour­fully: he was a jazz player and would do some­thing dif­fer­ent each time. {087-J10}
stories.why: The best work some­times comes from los­ing con­trol. Morrison’s plan did not sur­vive the pro­ducer, and his album was the bet­ter for it; nor was he, in the mo­ment, the best judge of what he had made.
stories.postscript: Varma pairs it with *Moondance*, Morrison with his own band, doing R&B the tra­di­tional way. {087-R02}

quiz.a: The sum of the squares of the first four primes: 4, 9, 25 and 49.

quiz.q: Why does Ajay Shah call Moore’s Law an economic law rather than a law of physics?
quiz.a: Nothing in na­ture guar­an­tees the dou­bling; it holds be­cause peo­ple keep pil­ing on in­no­va­tion and cap­i­tal.

quiz.q: What does Wright’s Law put on the x-axis, and what gain does it predict?
quiz.a: Cumulative life­time out­put; roughly a 20 per cent pro­duc­tiv­ity gain for every dou­bling.

quiz.q: What three things, according to Ajay Shah, does a CPU need to be able to do?
quiz.a: Fetch a mem­ory cell into a reg­is­ter, add, and branch on an if.

quiz.q: How much could any Ritz-Carlton employee spend on a guest without asking anyone, from 1983?
quiz.a: Up to $2,000, against a reg­u­lar guest’s life­time value of $200,000.

quiz.q: Which company in Holland bet a decade early on extreme ultraviolet lithography, and why?
quiz.a: ASML, which pro­jected Moore’s Law ten years ahead and saw con­ven­tional lithog­ra­phy max­ing out.

p4.credits: Everything is Everything was Amit Varma and Ajay Shah’s weekly show, 128 episodes from June 2023 to December 2025. This edition is made from Episode 87. The moving pictures, stills and chapter cards are from its video; the chapter art is by Simahina. Every play button starts the video at the moment it was said. The articles and headlines were written by Claude, an AI model, from the episode’s machine-made transcript, and checked against it. Other photographs are from Wikimedia Commons: Lawrence Summers (United States Department of Treasury, public domain); Gordon Moore (Intel Free Press, CC BY-SA 2.0); Paul R. Ehrlich (Ilka Hartmann, public domain); Prasanta Chandra Mahalanobis (Parinitha Ravi, CC BY-SA 4.0); Van Morrison (Art Siegel (artolog on flickr), CC BY-SA 2.0); Tom Robbins (48states (talk) (Uploads), public domain); Marianne Faithfull (London, public domain). The covers on the shelf are from Amazon, Apple and Spotify.

shelf.title: Astral Weeks
shelf.creator: Van Morrison
shelf.why: Van Morrison’s mas­ter­piece of deeply mov­ing songs, born when the pro­ducer re­placed his mu­si­cians with jazz play­ers, in­clud­ing bassist Richard Davis, who im­pro­vised around him.

shelf.title: Moondance
shelf.creator: Van Morrison
shelf.why: The coun­ter­point to Astral Weeks: Van Morrison with his own band, doing R&B the tra­di­tional way, ex­actly as he wanted.

shelf.title: Brown Eyed Girl
shelf.creator: Van Morrison
shelf.why: It is a play­ful bridge from tran­sis­tors on chips to the tran­sis­tor radio.

shelf.title: Madame George
shelf.creator: Van Morrison
shelf.why: One of Amit’s favourite songs of all time, ‘an ab­so­lutely epic’ song and the cen­tre­piece of Astral Weeks, an album he con­sid­ers a mas­ter­piece.

shelf.title: Madame George (Marianne Faithfull’s version)
shelf.creator: Marianne Faithfull
shelf.why: ‘A glo­ri­ous ethe­real cover’ of Van Morrison’s Madame George, one of the two great ver­sions Amit rec­om­mends along­side the orig­i­nal.

shelf.title: Madame George (Luka Bloom’s version)
shelf.creator: Luka Bloom
shelf.why: Another fan­tas­tic ver­sion of Van Morrison’s Madame George, by the Irish singer-songwriter Luka Bloom.

shelf.title: Episode 170 of A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
shelf.why: Amit calls it a great pod­cast episode on Astral Weeks that he had lis­tened to, for any­one who wants the full story be­hind the album.

shelf.title: Statistical Basis for Predicting Technological Progress
shelf.creator: Béla Nagy, J Doyne Farmer, Quan M Bui & Jessika E Trancik
shelf.why: He calls it a beau­ti­ful paper and mind-blowing data work.

shelf.title: Even Cowgirls Get the Blues
shelf.creator: Tom Robbins
shelf.why: Ajay quotes two lines from Tom Robbins’s novel: one re­minds him that peo­ple who seem prickly are usu­ally fine once you get going, the other that stag­na­tion is a mind­set, since only those who think they are on rou­tine flights are on them.

shelf.title: Ben Wolff’s X thread on Ritz-Carlton
shelf.creator: Ben Wolff
shelf.why: It col­lects the sto­ries of em­ploy­ees using $2,000 of dis­cre­tion, which il­lus­trate how in­cen­tives and trust cre­ate own­er­ship.

shelf.title: I, Pencil
shelf.creator: Leonard Read
shelf.why: A pen­cil nar­rates its own mak­ing from ma­te­ri­als and know-how scat­tered across many coun­tries, co­or­di­nated by prices with no one in charge.

shelf.title: Life Lessons
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Amit and Ajay’s course on what they wish they had been taught at twenty: learn­ing how to learn, frame­works for think­ing, writ­ing, prob­a­bilis­tic in­tu­ition, eco­nom­ics, the his­tory of thought, per­sonal fi­nance (Ajay’s mod­ule is ‘legendary’) and health.

shelf.title: Understanding India’s Pensions Disaster (Episode 65)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: A first-principles ac­count of pen­sion re­form: how a small com­mu­nity with a shared phi­los­o­phy built the NPS, and how guar­an­tees and the old mess re­turned once that com­mu­nity dis­persed and its knowl­edge faded.

shelf.title: Our Population Is Our Greatest Asset (Episode 20)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: The ar­gu­ment that peo­ple are brains, not stom­achs: hu­mans are in­no­va­tors whose cre­ativ­ity beats scarcity, so India’s prob­lem is too few chil­dren and too lit­tle train­ing of minds, not too many peo­ple.

shelf.title: The Case for Nuclear Electricity (Episode 78)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: The case for nu­clear power as a path out of fos­sil fuels: Amit calls it the safest form of en­ergy known and an ob­vi­ous an­swer to cli­mate change, point­ing to France, which at 71% nu­clear emits a tenth of the world av­er­age CO2 per kilo­watt hour.

shelf.title: The Brave New Future of Electricity (Episode 40)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Ajay’s mas­ter­class on the power sec­tor: solar, wind, stor­age and time-of-day pric­ing, why elec­tric­ity prices must be al­lowed to move, and why fix­ing Indian power is a 25-year jour­ney that Indian man­u­fac­tur­ing de­pends on.

shelf.title: The Heart of Disruption (Episode 86)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Why big com­pa­nies crum­ble when they can’t adapt and how some es­cape that fate, told through Netflix’s 2007 stream­ing bet and the first half of Amit’s own startup saga.

shelf.title: How Family Firms Evolve (Episode 34)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Original think­ing from Ajay on how Indian firms evolved over 30 years and how they should ma­ture: from fam­ily con­trol to dis­persed share­hold­ing, a pow­er­ful board and a man­age­ment team ac­count­able to it.

shelf.title: From Imperial to Adaptive Firms (Episode 37)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: How Indian firms moved from re­gional satraps in the 1980s to top-down ‘imperial’ firms with uni­form best prac­tices, and then to ‘adaptive’ firms that pair rules with local flex­i­bil­ity.

shelf.title: Graduating to Globalisation (Episode 48)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Ajay’s case that in­ter­na­tion­al­i­sa­tion is the en­gine of growth: com­pet­ing with the world forces firms to im­port best prac­tices and raise their game, and the gains spread through the econ­omy.

shelf.title: Going Bankrupt in India (Episode 80)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Why bank­ruptcy is a healthy, nor­mal part of eco­nomic life, and how the pol­i­tics of India’s bank­ruptcy re­form gave big com­pa­nies out­sized in­flu­ence, left op­er­a­tional cred­i­tors weak and squeezed small manufacturers’ work­ing cap­i­tal.

shelf.title: The Beauty of Finance (Episode 21)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Ajay’s mas­ter­class on why fi­nance ex­ists and why it mat­ters to the real econ­omy: fi­nance as ‘the brain of the economy’, not a casino for the rich, traced back to me­dieval trad­ing voy­ages.

laughs.text: The cold open is a ‘test of Ajay’s math skills’: the sum of the squares of the first four primes. Ajay adds 4, 9, 25 and 49 aloud and lands on 87, so Amit says ‘Welcome to episode eighty seven.’

Amit re­fuses to let Ajay sim­ply an­nounce an­other topic: ‘God knows how many episodes on firms you’ve got­ten away with and other in­ter­est­ing sub­jects like bank­ruptcy reg­u­la­tion.’ Ajay is in­ter­viewed like a job ap­pli­cant. ‘Applicant’s name.’ ‘Moore’s Laws.’ ‘Is your name Moore’s Laws?’ ‘My fa­ther was Mr. Laws.’ Age fifty-nine, oc­cu­pa­tion YouTuber. His pitch be­gins: ‘There’s a great wild west wind tear­ing through this mod­ern world and it is called CPUs.’ It ends with the ques­tion of whether the form must be sub­mit­ted in trip­li­cate: ‘Yes, why not... in phys­i­cal copies.’
Amit: ‘Bollywood has al­ways been fas­ci­nated by log graphs... there are songs about it.’ It is a pun on ‘log’, the Hindi word for ‘people’.

After the chess­board para­ble, Ajay works out the rice in kilo­grams against the mass of the earth and con­cludes it is ‘well be­yond the re­sources of any king.’ Amit shrugs: ‘Doesn’t mat­ter. It’s a lot of grain.’

Ajay: ‘for all ye cal­low gen­tle read­ers that are used to squan­der­ing like bil­lions of tran­sis­tors in the CPUs on your phones, I will have you know... the Intel 4004 had some­thing like 2300 tran­sis­tors.’

On dial-up days, Amit re­calls hav­ing ‘half a pic­ture of Samantha Fox’ when the con­nec­tion drops and the screen says buffer­ing, while the edit plays the modem sound: ‘Just as you are see­ing now, gen­tle reader, we are so smart.’ Ajay tops it: ‘I could lis­ten to the ne­go­ti­a­tion of the modem and I would know which pro­to­col it got through.’

Amit ap­plies Wright’s Law to the show: ‘when we make episode one sev­enty four will be twenty per­cent bet­ter than we are now.’ Ajay agrees, and notes the bulk of the gains came early and ‘now the learn­ing rate has gone down.’
In the Ritz-Carlton story, Amit re­fuses to call Thomas the Tank Engine a toy be­cause that would in­sult Thomas, and adds that the hotel sent pho­tos of Thomas en­joy­ing spa treat­ment.

Asked by Van Morrison decades later to re­play his Astral Weeks bass lines ex­actly, Richard Davis replies, as Amit tells it: ‘No, you fucker, I’m a jazz player, I’ll do some­thing dif­fer­ent each time.’

The para­ble of the king and the chess­board: one grain of rice on the first square, dou­bled on each square after, which be­comes an im­pos­si­ble amount by the 64th. It is used to show the power of dou­bling.
Kaun Banega Crorepati: the quiz show was be­com­ing a hit in 2000, which is the con­text for Amit build­ing his on­line quiz game.

‘Classic Mahalanobis-based kind of thinking’: Ajay’s short­hand for the planner’s be­lief that only a co­er­cive gov­ern­ment can co­or­di­nate a com­plex in­dus­try, which the semi­con­duc­tor world dis­proves.
Ajay’s riff on Leonard Read’s essay: ‘I, Pencil does not hold a can­dle to I, CPU.’

Transistor ra­dios as the ‘killer app’ of the old days, glued to people’s ears for cricket com­men­tary. Amit notes that a generation’s mem­o­ries of Sunil Gavaskar’s straight drive, or of Marshall being hit, were imag­ined from com­men­tary and later retro­fit­ted onto footage.
